newsitem.title: THAILAND: Key data shows Thai economy flagging further.
newsitem.headline: Key data shows Thai economy flagging further.

text.p: Key Thai economic monthly indicators released by the central bank on Thursday showed that the country's sluggish economy was slowing further and a bottom had yet to be reached, the bank's chief economist said.

Analysts told Reuters the lethargic economy could pose further threats to the already reeling Thai financial sector which last month was given a major revamp by authorities, and could hurt the depressed property sector further.

Bank of Thailand chief economist Kleothong Hetrakul told reporters after the data was released that the manufacturing index and private investment growth both showed further signs of slowing in March.

Private investment growth in February slid to 6.3 percent from 6.8 percent year on year, while the manufacturing production index plunged to 2.4 percent in February from 4.2 percent in January, latest Bank of Thailand data showed.

But Thailand's external balances picture showed some signs of improvement. The current account deficit narrowed to one of its lowest recorded points in recent years, while the trade deficit also shrunk, Kleothong said.
Central bank data showed the country posted a current account deficit of 14.7 billion baht ($560 million) in February, against 22.5 billion baht in January.
The trade deficit narrowed in February to 21.7 billion baht from 39 billion baht a month earlier, mostly due to a plunge in imports rather than an improvement in exports.
"Economic stability is quite satisfactory. The current account deficit for the whole of 1997 could fall below six percent of gross domestic product," Kleothong said.
"The average deficit during the first two months of this year was about 19 billion baht compared with the average of more than 30 billion baht per month last year."

Exports, which showed some improvement in January, contracted 5.5 percent year-on-year in February to a total value of 108.6 billion baht. Imports slid to 130.3 billion baht in February from 154.9 billion in January -- an 11 percent drop year-on-year.

"We are seing some improvement in the external sector but there is some damage to the domestic economy. High rates are slowing manufacturing activity and weakening consumer spending," said the chief representative of a U.S. investment bank.

Thailand's economy is officially forecast to grow 6.8 percent this year, but analysts said recent turmoil in the financial sector, high interest rates and a cash-strapped property sector could cap growth to well below six percent.
Thai financial institutions have billions of dollars in bad loans to the property sector which has been hit by a glut and high rates.

Last month, financial institutions were ordered by authorities to raise provisioning against poor-quality assets and the government said it would launch 100 billion baht in zero coupon bonds to raise funds to help the property sector.

"We don't expect any change for the Thai economy unless high rates start falling. That can only happen if the central bank is prepared to lower them and not just use them to defend the baht," the investment bank's chief representative said.
Sriyan Pietersz, strategist at Capital Nomura Securities, said most investors were now focusing on the state of the economy rather than on the external picture after recent financial turmoil.

"If the economy slows it will make it harder for local financial institutions to perform well, loan quality could deteriorate and the weak corporate sector could bring down the stock market," he said.
